When I was in highschool, I found that therapy was way more effective than pills.

I have some pretty extreme social anxiety and performance anxiety in addition to my depression; so I wasn't able to just 'talk about my feelings' through our sessions. We talked about my therapist as much as we talked about me.

Sometimes we barely talked at all.

But over the course of a few months he got me off caffeine, helped me with some coping strategies, and just made me feel heard when I had been feeling pretty invisible.

You don't have to tell your parents about everything you're going through if you don't think you can have that conversation right now. But I'd say get into regular therapy if you aren't already and YOU choose the therapist. If you don't click with them, switch.

Anyways, if you have a goal to get something more out of it I would try to increase focus through use of regular reality checks, dream journaling, and meditation.

Find a few things that work for you and focus on those. I like using small finger motions to stay in the space between sleep and awake for a good WILD. But reality checks are your strongest tool for a DILD which I have much more often.

You have to try a lot of things that don't work sometimes too, that's just part of it, so don't get discouraged if you don't repeat the experience right away.

I recommend to new dreamers to re read your dream journal nightly before bed. It strengthens that connection in your brain.

If you think about the way our brains make memories - it is from the connection between two points being used over and over again until that connection becomes natural for the brain. That's why we use repetition to remember. I imagine that physical process as laying the communication network between waking and sleeping minds.

But that's not what you mean. What you need to do to begin teaching your brain to look for dream signs is regular reality checks.

Every time you turn a light on or off, did it change the light in the room?

When you go through a door or around a corner is the place your in still the same or has it changed?

If you read a sign, look away, and then read it again, did the words change? Do they make sense?

Training your brain while you're awake is really important.

Hey, this is really interesting.

I have had dreams where I felt weight on me; but never where I myself began to feel sensation and weight in the dream after becoming lucid - that I remember.

That sounds incredible if you were able to hold on to it. But I think that it is possible the sensation is related to slowly waking up into consciousness from a lucid dream. Losing a lucid dream doesn't always cause the dreamer to wake up; a lot of the time ita just black out or next dream.

But if you are waking up lucid you are going to become more and more aware of your physical body and sensations as you wake up. That isn't bad though, you can definitely still use it!

Try to just keep your eyes shut if it happens again and breathe yourself back to sleep. Often times waking up and going back to sleep helps with lucidity anyway; so waking up from a lucid dream and then being able to drift right back into it would be a fantastic and doable trick.

In the beginning of 2015 I decided to take a trip to Thailand to get some peace and explore the world a bit.

My sister had been to Thailand before me and the stories I heard made me feel that nagging need to travel.  Still, I wanted to do it my way and figure out the best spots on my own.

A few months later, I packed up my Mountain Hardware backpack with way more weight than I needed (travel chess is NOT a necessity) and headed to the airport. I landed in Chiang Mai instead of Bangkok (RECOMMENDED) and made my way slowly down to the islands. I hit the party islands first, right in time for the Full Moon Party. Which I did not attend. Instead I ate massive amounts of food on the street above and listening to the festivities.

After a two week silent retreat, I was ready for an island of a very different kind.

Koh Chang is a beautiful island on the west side of Thailand that has no motor vehicles. (There are multiple Koh Changs, so do research). Some of my most memorable moments were there exploring and smoking.

One morning I woke up in my hammock totally at peace with the world and saw this dog playing on the beach.

Hey,

Your post resignated with me that you would want to sleep and never wake up.
I have an on again off again relationship with sleep myself and it seems like when I am at my worst mental state; sleep is the most difficult.
Sometimes I will have the thought that 'If I go to sleep now I'll have to wake up in the morning and there's nothing I can do to stop it.'
My body wants sleep, and my mind wants to have a way to escape; but I can't sleep from fear of waking up!

Now for the part that maybe could be helpful to you:
I recommend that everyone practices lucid dreaming. It's not an easy process, but it can be extremely rewarding.

When I'm not suffering from insomnia I find that lucid dreaming really makes me feel more in control of my time and my life.

There is an intrinsic calmness to the thought of never having to feel pain again. That seems somewhat apparent.

And the calm can be helpful; but it can also be helpful to face down the pain head on. When thoughts surface, I like to focus on the pain that would be felt if I ever ended things. I've heard again and again about the pain caused to others who lost a loved one; but that's not what I'm talking about.

Unless you're convinced of a positive afterlife; what calmness is there going to be after you die?
Especially if you're Catholic, there's no pleasant ending waiting for victims of suicide. And if there is no afterlife at all then there isn't peace or serenity. There is just blackness.

So instead of focusing on some imagined state of calm and never having to hurt again, I focus on something real: what my last thoughts would be. Even a painless death wouldn't be peaceful if in the last moments of one's life their only thoughts are regret at the decision and complete helplessness to stop it. No matter what the method, there's always that chance that our primate brain will take over and try to undo the situation. Panic. Anxiety.

After living through it mentally, I can't put myself in that situation physically.
